name: concepts-readroom-explore-2/tank
refs: THE POD (project-owned game art): a wild seed pod, slate-blue with a round coral cap, pale vertical ribs and coral dots. Keep its design exactly wherever a pod appears; never make it a jar, a vase, a lantern or an egg of another design.

THE CREATURE (project-owned game art): the Loika the pod will become: a small round charcoal creature with a cream belly and muzzle, amber eyes, four stubby legs with pale toes and three green leaves on its head. Keep its design exactly; never invent another creature.

THE STATION'S FINISH (one of our own screens, project-owned): its incubator, a matte dark slate capsule with a glass dome, a warm lamp inside and a moss nest, standing on a quiet sage wall with soft painted light. Take the rendering: matte, soft, warm, painted, real depth, a handled instrument. Today's incubator is this capsule; the new one in the picture may be of the same family but of the concept's own form.

THE STATION'S HOUSING (one of our own screens, project-owned): the sage powder-coated housing with recessed screws, a braided black hose with brass fittings, and the dark soft tray inside where the pod stands. This is the material language of every instrument in the picture: sage and sand housing, dark rubber, screws, braided hose, dark matte slate displays. Take the materials, not the layout.
prompt:
Paint the WHOLE screen of a creature-keeping game played on a handheld home research station, 16:9, a mood-and-layout thumbnail for a concept: the READING ROOM, where the player reads a wild pod (a seed pod with a creature's genome sleeping inside) one chapter at a time, as an EXPERIMENT on a research bench. The feeling: a pod is RICH IN SURPRISES, there is more inside than can be seen, and each read brings one out into the light. The place is a LAB THAT IS A HOME: a naturalist's field kit on a warm evening, cosy because it is handled and loved, never a cold laboratory, never a cottage. ALSO IN THE PICTURE, smaller, the station's INCUBATORS as the same family of instrument as the reading instrument (same housing, same materials, same maker), two or three units on the same bench and a free mount or bay where another unit could be added: one incubator holds a glowing bud growing in warm light, one is empty and dark, the free mount has only its hose fitting. CONCEPT: THE TANK (a specimen tank with sensors). A round glass tank in a sage frame fills the centre of the screen, filled with clear warm water that glows softly, and the pod rests in the middle of it on a dark pad, lit from within. Around the pod, clipped to the tank's rim in a ring, several small sage sensor probes with dark rubber grips lean in, each with a tiny lamp, and from one probe a soft ripple spreads through the water and where the ripple passes a soft picture forms in the water, a lock of russet fur, with a fainter second ring behind it. The water is full of many tiny drifting lit motes in different soft colours (russet, amber, cream, ash, green), like plankton: the unread chapters, a tank rich with them. The small Loika sits on the bench at the lower right pressing its nose to the glass, half painted in colour and half soft grey fog. To the left, smaller, the family's incubators: two smaller round tanks in the same frames, one lit warm with a bud floating inside, one dark and drained, and a bare ring mount with a braided hose fitting.
LIGHT AND FINISH: one warm key light from the top left, soft cast shadows, soft contact shadows, a few small lit marks on the instruments that mean something (a lamp on a working unit, nothing lit for show). Matte, painted, miniature finish like the reference screens; the instruments are quiet matte sage, sand, dark rubber and dark slate; the colour lives in the pod's inner light, the surprises and the life. No gloss, no chrome, no neon, no holograms, no glowing outlines, no sci-fi interface, nothing childish, no wooden furniture, no books, no candles, no cottage.
NO text, letters, digits, numbers, logos, buttons, panels or icons anywhere (the game types its words later). No frame, no border, no vignette; the picture fills the canvas edge to edge.
